description: We are a team of software engineering students aiming for the moon.
summary: Homestead is a browser game where a crew of up to four players, or one solo player, designs a space mission and then has to live with it. Mission Control hands the crew a survey job on the Moon or Mars and a budget, but no spacecraft. They have five minutes to scavenge a launch campus for parts, or buy them from a kiosk catalog, and fill four slots: propulsion, power, comms and payload. Each of the twenty parts is based on real NASA hardware, from Dawn's ion drive to Curiosity's MMRTG. Six meters on the rocket's blueprint show the trade-offs between mass, power, data, uplink, flight time and budget. Then the crew flies what it built. The Pilot, Rocket Engineer, Comms Engineer and Science Officer each run their own station, and the mounted parts decide how hard each one is. On the surface they work through Mission Control's list through dust storms or solar flares before the extraction ship arrives. Every run ends with a mission report that traces the biggest loss back to the part that caused it, and names the real hardware that made the same trade. The challenge asks for a game where every decision has a consequence and players learn why a mission succeeded or failed. Homestead turns a mission design trade study into about fifteen minutes of play for people with no space background, in any browser, even on a phone.
details:
Overview

Homestead is a cooperative browser game about space mission design. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by presenting a mission trade study as play: players select subsystems under mass, power, budget and time constraints, then operate the resulting spacecraft and see the consequences of each choice. A run lasts about 15 minutes and supports one to four players. It requires no installation and runs on desktop browsers and on phones and tablets.

Structure of a run

  1. Brief. Mission Control assigns a survey of the Moon or Mars. The mission card gives the travel time, radio delay, budget and data target. Moon: about 3 days, 1.3 second radio delay, 20 credits, 33 data units. Mars: about 7 months, 3 to 22 minute radio delay, about 43 percent of Earth's sunlight, 40 credits, 50 data units.
  2. Build (5 minutes). The crew collects parts on a launch campus and mounts them in four slots: propulsion, power, communications and payload. Parts spawn from a shared seed, so layouts differ between runs. Parts can also be bought from a kiosk catalog at full cost; parts found on the campus count at half cost. The mission budget acts as a cost cap that reduces the score when exceeded but does not prevent launch. A blueprint shows six meters (mass, power, data, uplink, flight time and budget), and each part can be inspected for its specifications and the hardware it is based on. Slots left empty when time expires receive low-performance salvage parts.
  3. Flight (about 2 to 4.5 minutes, depending on destination and engine). Each player operates one station. The Pilot steers through debris; handling depends on the engine. The Rocket Engineer keeps the power bus below its supply limit and repairs hull breaches. The Comms Engineer keeps the antenna pointed at Earth; a stable link gives the Pilot advance warning of debris. The Science Officer regulates energy core temperature and cabin oxygen. Seeded events include debris fields, power surges, solar flares, core temperature spikes and course corrections. Loss of hull integrity or cabin oxygen ends the run.
  4. Surface (5 minutes). Three objectives are drawn each run from a pool: scanning rich sites, returning a sample, deploying an instrument, drilling for ice, aligning a relay antenna with an orbiter, and cleaning solar panels (solar builds only). Each is a short minigame. Data counts toward the target only after it is uplinked from the lander. Suit oxygen and power drain away from the lander and recharge at it. Additional events include suit malfunctions, a lander relay fault and micrometeorite strikes. Crews that complete their objectives early can vote to call the extraction ship.
  5. Mission report. The report presents the run in five stages, identifies the part most responsible for the largest loss, traces the chain of events that followed from it, cites the real mission that faced the same trade-off, and gives the score.

A tutorial introduces each phase and each flight station the first time a player reaches it.

Parts and sources

The game has 20 parts, each modelled on NASA flight hardware. Mass and power follow the hardware; costs follow real cost ratios scaled to the mission budgets. All values are stored in a single data file.

  • Propulsion: solid motor (180 kg, lifts 600 kg; Space Shuttle and SLS boosters), chemical engine (300 kg, lifts 900 kg; RL10), storable engine (260 kg, lifts 800 kg; Orion service module engine), ion drive (120 kg, lifts 500 kg, 250 W; Dawn), Hall thruster (140 kg, lifts 550 kg, 350 W; Psyche).
  • Power: small solar array (60 kg, 300 W; InSight), roll-out solar array (70 kg, 550 W; ROSA on the ISS and DART), large solar array (150 kg, 600 W; Juno), radioisotope generator (110 kg, 450 W; MMRTG on Curiosity and Perseverance), fission reactor (230 kg, 800 W; Kilopower KRUSTY test).
  • Communications: low-gain antenna (rover low-gain antennas), CubeSat reflectarray (MarCO), UHF relay radio (Electra on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and the rovers), high-gain dish (MRO 3 m dish), laser terminal (Deep Space Optical Communications on Psyche).
  • Payload: neutron spectrometer (Lunar Prospector and LEND), camera (HiRISE), spectrometer (SuperCam), radar sounder (SHARAD), sample lab (SAM on Curiosity).

Mission card values come from NASA Moon and Mars fact pages and the NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet. Hardware references come from NASA mission pages. The repository README lists every source.

Consequence model

Each subsystem choice affects later phases.

  • Mass. Total mass, including a 200 kg crew cabin, is compared with the engine's lift. A rocket heavier than its lift capacity does not reach orbit.
  • Power. The flight power bus carries a 150 W base load (life support, heating and lighting) plus each part's draw. If draw exceeds supply for 4 seconds, the breaker trips and all systems are unpowered for 4 seconds.
  • Solar power. Solar output decreases to 60 percent during transit to Mars, and solar flares reduce it to 55 percent for 11 seconds. Radioisotope and fission sources are unaffected. On Mars, solar arrays recharge suits at 43 percent of their nominal rate, matching the planet's share of Earth's sunlight.
  • Communications. The antenna determines pointing difficulty, debris warning time (2 seconds for the low-gain antenna, 6 for the laser terminal) and uplink rate.
  • Payload. The instrument determines data per scan and the rate at which the energy core heats during flight.
  • Hazards. Mars has three dust storms per surface phase, each announced 8 seconds in advance, which increase suit drain fourfold. The Moon has three solar flares, each announced 10 seconds in advance, which increase suit drain sixfold for players not sheltered at the lander or behind a rock. A suit that lasts about 2.5 minutes in the open lasts under 40 seconds inside a storm.

Worked example (Mars)

An ion drive, radioisotope generator, high-gain dish and camera give a total mass of 530 kg against the ion drive's 500 kg lift. The build screen warns that the rocket will not reach orbit; if it is launched anyway, the report identifies the engine and explains mass margins.

Replacing the ion drive with the chemical engine gives 710 kg against 900 kg of lift and a power draw of 300 W against 450 W of supply, unaffected by flares or dust. Bought entirely at the kiosk, this build costs 38 of the 40 credits available.

Substituting a small solar array for the generator saves 12 credits and matches the 300 W draw on the pad. During transit, however, output falls to 180 W, causing repeated breaker trips unless the Engineer sheds loads, and suit recharge on the surface falls from 11 to about 3 percent per second. The report then cites InSight, whose solar arrays were gradually covered by dust until the mission ended.

Scoring

The score weights mission success first: up to 500 points for data uplinked against the target, 160 for a crew still standing at extraction, 2 per unspent credit, up to 180 for build time remaining, up to 40 for fuel and hull at arrival, 20 per objective and 30 for the bonus objective.

Multiplayer

In solo play, one player holds all four flight roles. Online, one player hosts and up to three others join with a six-character code; the four roles are divided among them. The host runs the simulation and distributes its state, so all clients agree. A shared seed fixes parts, events and hazards, which allows different crews to attempt the same mission.

Benefits and intended impact

The game is aimed at students and newcomers with no background in spaceflight. It introduces the core of mission design, trading mass, power, budget, data and time against a mission objective, in a single session suited to a classroom period. Because there is no single correct build, each run ends on one identified trade-off linked to a real mission, such as the choice between solar and radioisotope power or between a light antenna and a high-gain dish. Shared seeds let a class or several teams attempt the same mission and compare their decisions. The intended impact is that players leave with a working understanding of why real missions choose the subsystems they do.

Novelty

Mission design is usually taught through worksheets and spreadsheet trade studies. Homestead places the same trade study under time pressure and then makes the crew operate the result, so each design decision is experienced as a later consequence rather than read as a number. Splitting the spacecraft into four stations, each visible only to its operator, requires the crew to communicate in the way a mission team does. The report closes the loop by tracing the outcome back to a single design choice and a real precedent.

Design considerations

  • Scientific grounding against playability. Part mass, power and hardware references follow NASA sources, while flight and surface rules are simplified so that a full mission fits in about 15 minutes.
  • Every choice must matter. A part was only included if it changes something in a later phase.
  • Access. The game runs in a browser with no installation, supports phones and tablets, can be played solo, and teaches its controls through an in-game tutorial.
  • Fairness and repeatability. A shared seed determines parts, events and hazards, so results can be compared between crews.
  • Infrastructure. Online play is host-based over peer-to-peer connections, so the game has no server cost; solo play does not depend on the network.
  • Competition rules. AI use is acknowledged in the repository, no NASA logos or mission insignia are used, and all outside resources are credited with their licences.

Implementation

  • Software. The game is written in JavaScript on HTML5 Canvas, with all sprites drawn procedurally as pixel art. Online play uses a TypeScript networking layer built on PeerJS and WebRTC, with no dedicated server. The project is built with Vite and hosted on itch.io. Hardware. No special hardware is required; the game was developed on standard laptops and runs on any device with a modern browser.
  • Process. A team of six developed it, each member responsible for one area, with all changes merged through pull requests. The networking layer has automated tests, and the game was tested in full solo and two-player runs after merges.

Source code: https://github.com/TadeyRuk/Homestead

Limitations and future work

Flight, power and drag are simplified game rules rather than physical simulation; part mass and power follow real hardware, while flight and surface values are game assumptions. The game covers two destinations. Online play depends on network conditions, as some networks block direct peer connections; solo play is unaffected. Future work includes additional missions and parts, a classroom mode with a shared seed, and accessibility options such as colour-blind palettes and remappable controls.
